bp.title: Inside the fly's brain
bp.lead: Your opponent is the wiring of a real fruit fly, mapped cell by cell under an electron microscope. Before every move the board is shown to it, the signal spreads through its neurons for ten steps, and the move is read out from the result. This page shows that happening.
bp.stat.readout: neurons the move is read from
bp.stage.title: What you are looking at
bp.stage.body: Each visible dot is a neuron with a measured cell-body position. Neurons without a recorded position are hidden. Press play to watch ten steps of simulated activity. Drag to turn the brain; scroll to zoom.
bp.region.0: The optic lobes. The board enters here, through the neurons of the eye.
bp.region.1: Neurons carrying what the eyes saw into the brain.
bp.region.2: Where most of the combining happens: learning and memory centres, and everything in between.
bp.region.3: Descending and motor neurons, the ones that would move the fly's body.
bp.region.4: Ascending neurons carrying signals into the brain.
bp.region.5: Touch, taste, smell and the rest. Here they receive facts about the game: castling, check, material.
bp.how.title: How a move is made
bp.how.see.title: It sees
bp.how.see.body: The board reaches 22,586 visual neurons: piece locations, attacks and en passant. A separate input carries the game state.
bp.how.spread.title: The signal spreads
bp.how.spread.body: For ten steps, each simulated neuron passes activity along the measured graph. Trained gains and biases shape the response.
bp.how.read.title: Instinct is read out
bp.how.read.body: A trained readout combines 7,526 neurons into preferences for legal moves and a judgement of the current position.
bp.how.choose.title: It imagines and chooses
bp.how.choose.body: DROSO-1 explores promising continuations with its own policy and position value. Scout uses 8 simulations, Tactician 32 and Thinker 64; a game clock can stop the search sooner.
bp.flow.body: The same recording, per region. A line means one region is driving another right now; the thicker and busier, the stronger. Red is inhibition, a brake rather than a push. Gold lines lead to the neurons the move is read from.
bp.thoughts.body: The moves the fly considered for its last decision. The bar is its instinct; the number is how good the move looked after imagining the replies (in pawns, from the fly's side).
bp.sees.body: The board arrives from the side to move: own pieces, opposing pieces, both attack maps and the en passant target. The trained input map covers all 64 squares.
bp.faq.title: Good to know
bp.faq.real.q: Is this a real fly brain?
bp.faq.real.a: The graph comes from FlyWire v783, a reconstruction of a female fruit fly’s brain. Connections with fewer than five synapses are filtered out. The activity is a mathematical simulation on that graph.
bp.faq.learned.a: The strength of each connection, a bias per neuron, how the board reaches the eyes, and the small readout. Who connects to whom was never changed.
bp.faq.strength.a: Thinker scored about 1500 in a 64-game probe against Stockfish 19 limited to 1320 and 1500, at depth 8. The model used 64 simulations without a clock; the estimate’s 95% interval was 1410–1603. This is a test-specific result, not a FIDE or website rating. Scout and Tactician have no separate rating probe.
bp.faq.learning.q: Does it learn from our games?
bp.faq.learning.a: No. The brain is fixed after training; your games only make it think, they do not change it.
